text: Most SOCs organize analyst work into three tiers, and each tier has a real, distinct job rather than just a different pay grade. Tier 1 is the first set of eyes on the queue. Tier 2 goes deeper once something's escalated. Tier 3 doesn't wait for alerts at all. Knowing which tier does what is the difference between reading a job posting and actually understanding this career path.

Tier 1 monitors the alert queue, does enough initial investigation to tell a true positive from a false positive, and either closes an alert with notes or escalates it. Tier 2 takes those escalations, with broader access and tooling to investigate deeper, and makes the real call — then performs the actual containment and incident response. Tier 3 proactively hunts for compromise that never triggered any rule, and tunes the detection tooling itself.

A SIEM raises an alert: failed logins, then a success. Tier 1 checks the user's normal device and location, finds nothing conclusive, and escalates. Tier 2 checks the source IP against threat intelligence, confirms it's tied to known botnet infrastructure, pulls endpoint telemetry, and isolates the machine. Later, Tier 3 notices the technique wasn't fully covered and builds a new correlation rule to catch it earlier next time.

This course trains realistically for the Tier 1 seat — triage, investigation fundamentals, and the SIEM mechanics the rest of this chapter and the next one cover. The typical real-world path from there is Tier 1 for roughly one to two years building investigation judgment on real alerts, then Tier 2 once that judgment is demonstrated, then Tier 3 or a specialized role like detection engineering after further experience.

That's this course's own path: student, then a real Tier 1 seat, then Tier 2 and beyond, building on exactly the skills this lesson just broke down. Up next, Lesson 3 covers how a SOC actually staffs that queue around the clock — the shift models and 24x7 coverage behind who's watching at 3 a.m.
